brief: Goldman's Mark Wilson frames Thursday's 4.9-standard-deviation Nasdaq 100 crash, a move that should occur roughly once every 8,000 years under a normal distribution, as the product of market structure, not news: over half of stocks are passively owned, a large share of volume is non-fundamental, and the fastest fundamental managers run similarly leveraged, similarly risk-modeled strategies. A shrinking pool of price-sensitive capital plus a similarly-behaving fast-money cohort produces moves the standard distribution doesn't predict; when one pod hits a stop, they all do, leaving only price-agnostic passive and systematic sellers on the other side. Nomura's McElligott sized Thursday's flows at $47bn of levered-ETF selling and $61bn of vol-control supply; Goldman's desk put ETFs at 32% of the tape. Fundamental TMT funds lost 410bps, wiping out the group's entire 2026 gain. Goldman Prime shows nine straight days of de-grossing and net leverage at an 18-month low, which Wilson reads as bullish for a bounce, since the same structure that forces fast selling forces fast buying back, but the underlying fragility (passive ownership, ETF share, risk models) is unfixed, so another 4.9-sigma day is only a matter of time. The house view: a clean-positioning bounce is likely but will be as fast and crowded as the crash, complicated by a hot payrolls print reviving December rate-hike risk.
